messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early,
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component,
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central.
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
David Miller, a thirty-four-year-old school counselor, had always prided himself on being the calm, reliable presence students could turn to. That sense of self shattered six months ago on a field trip to a local park. He had turned away for what felt like a split second to answer a colleague’s question, and in that moment, a ten-year-old boy named Liam darted into the street. The car struck him with a sickening thud. David was the first to reach him, kneeling in the spreading pool of blood, holding Liam’s hand while shouting for an ambulance. The boy survived, but with severe pelvic fractures and internal injuries that required three surgeries and months of inpatient rehabilitation. The police investigation found no fault—Liam had bolted suddenly, and David’s actions after were appropriate—but David himself had come to a different verdict.

In the weeks that followed, the smell of antiseptic at the hospital became a doorway he could not close; whenever he passed a cleaning cart or walked into a doctor’s office, the odor pulled him back so vividly that he could feel the warm wetness on his knees and hear Liam’s small whimpers, as if it were happening all over again. The memory did not feel like a memory—it was a full sensory reliving, complete with the screech of tires and the metallic smell of blood, and he could never find the words to describe it to his wife without his throat closing up. That reliving brought a surge of shame so powerful his heart would pound and his palms would sweat, and he began to dread bedtime because his body refused to relax—he stayed alert to every creak of the house, as if danger might arrive any second. The guilt was the worst part; he was certain that the accident had happened because of the way he had acted, because he had looked away, and that certainty wormed into everything: he started to doubt his judgment even in small decisions, convinced that he could not trust himself to do the right thing. His life, he believed, had been destroyed by that single moment.

To survive his daily routine, David developed strategies that he knew were not healthy but felt necessary. He kept his mind occupied all the time, listening to podcasts during his commute and humming under his breath during staff meetings, because any quiet moment let the memory slip in. When he had to drive past the police station near his office, he took a longer route, even though no officer had ever blamed him; the sight of a squad car made his stomach drop. He tried never to think about the event directly, but the harder he pushed it away, the more it seemed to ambush him. For instance, during a routine fire drill at school, the sudden noise and commotion—a common trigger of stress—sent his mind spiraling back to the field trip, and he had to excuse himself to the restroom to breathe. The more he blamed himself, the more hypervigilant he became at work, scanning the playground for any risk until his eyes ached. And the more he used mental distraction to block the memory, the more the memory seemed to intrude when he least expected it—sitting at dinner, the flash of a red car outside his window would bring the whole scene back, leaving him silent and shaking.

His attempts to manage his inner world started to affect his outer one. His wife noticed he was irritable, that he avoided telling her about his day, that he stayed up late watching television to avoid the insomnia caused by his need to stay alert. He missed his son’s soccer game because he had taken the long route to avoid a hospital and gotten stuck in traffic. At work, his colleagues remarked that he seemed distracted, and the school’s principal gently suggested he take some personal leave. David agreed, but being at home only gave him more time to ruminate. The quiet of his house became a trigger: any small stress—a dripping faucet, his wife sighing—set off the thought that he had failed, that one moment of inattention had proven he was untrustworthy, and then the memory would flood back with unbearable intensity.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when he could not get out of bed. He lay there, staring at the ceiling, thinking that his life really was destroyed, that he had ruined his own career and his family’s peace. He called a therapist that afternoon not because he believed he could be fixed, but because he was terrified that if he did not do something, the loop would never stop. He did not know if talking would help—he could barely put the event into words—but he was also afraid of what might happen if he stayed silent.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause triggers (e.g., that self-blame makes stimuli become reminders).
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat causes the trauma memory to appear. Threat is a consequence of memory, not a cause.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, distraction) lead to negative appraisals about oneself.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph indicates that maladaptive strategies cause triggers to arise or become more salient.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies produce a heightened sense of threat; threat seems to precede or accompany strategies.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
His life, he believed, had been destroyed by that single moment.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once he had concluded that he was at fault, ordinary moments of distraction in his work—a student calling his name unexpectedly, a door slamming—could feel like the moment his attention slipped again, pulling him straight back to the accident.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more he blamed himself, the more hypervigilant he became at work, scanning the playground for any risk until his eyes ached.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
On his most vigilant days, when he was scanning every corner of the playground, the memory of Liam's face would surface without warning—as if his body had already braced for disaster and the memory was the shape it took.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
For instance, during a routine fire drill at school, the sudden noise and commotion—a common trigger of stress—sent his mind spiraling back to the field trip, and he had to excuse himself to the restroom to breathe.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time he had to flee a situation that reminded him of the accident, a quiet part of him concluded that he was more fragile than his colleagues, that he could not handle what other people handled every day.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When he had to drive past the police station near his office, he took a longer route, even though no officer had ever blamed him; the sight of a squad car made his stomach drop.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The longer route itself became a daily acknowledgment of the accident—he could not drive that way without the thought of the police station, and then the accident, arriving right on schedule.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He kept his mind occupied all the time, listening to podcasts during his commute and humming under his breath during staff meetings, because any quiet moment let the memory slip in.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But the constant mental noise kept his nervous system on edge, as if the very need to block out the memory proved that danger was always near, ready to strike if he let his guard down.
<<<END>>>
